funding_code: (GRANT ONLY) RAVG PRE-DEVELOPMENT GRANT - WATER AND WASTE
naics_industry_sector: Utilities
project_announced_description: This Rural Development investment will evaluate wastewater management systems in the rural Alaskan villages of Nulato, Thorne Bay and Tuntutuliak. In Nulato, residents use honey buckets for wastewater disposal and lack sanitary methods to dispose of waste. There is a watering point located by the school and the laundromat, but its a challenge for some of the residents with no transportation to access these sanitation facilities as the new town-site is approximately two miles from the Old Town-site. In Thorne Bay, the community wastewater flow increases from about 50,000 gallons per day during dry periods to about 400,000 gallons per day during storm or rain events. The final lift station runs non-stop during rain events. The assigned Remote Maintenance Worker observed final lift station overflow during 2019 as pumps could not keep up with storm event infiltration. A bigger lift station pump is not practical as flow generated thereby would exceed the already strained wastewater plant treatment capacity that occurs during rain events. The collection system consists of five lift stations and 110 concrete manholes. Condition of four of the lift station is poor as the control systems are not functioning. The Harbor lift station is in good shape as it was part of the recently completed Harbor Improvement Project. One lift station is manually operated daily, though the terminal lift station operates by means of floats. No regulatory approval for the Tuntutuliak lagoon, which was developed in a tundra pond, has been located. The lagoon is immediately across the boardwalk from a landfill, causing comingling of waste.

funding_code: (GRANT ONLY) RAVG PRE-DEVELOPMENT GRANT - WATER AND WASTE
naics_industry_sector: Utilities
project_announced_description: This Rural Development investment will allow seven rural communities to provide grants to compromised sanitation/utility facilities. The City of Deering is served by a piped vacuum sewer system and a water haul system with water storage tanks at each home. The existing vacuum plant and vacuum sewer collection piping began operation in 1998. Wastewater treatment is provided by a single-cell facultative wastewater stabilization pond (non-aerated lagoon). The lagoon was originally intended to function as a percolating lagoon but does not appear to be percolating at this time. Sadly, the lagoon is periodically discharged by pumping to the offshore marine environment (Kotzebue Sound) under a State of Alaska discharge permit and mixing zone. The lagoon was designed, permitted and constructed for a population of 250 at 50-gallons per capita per day (gpcd). The problem is the single-cell configuration does not meet current lagoon design standards. Furthermore, the wastewater lagoon does not have a complete perimeter security fence. To make matters worse, the lagoon has experienced a degradation and partial failure of its earthen berm at the southwest corner. This is allowing wastewater to leach out from the lagoon, causing a health and safety risk to residents, particularly in conjunction with the incomplete security fencing. Simply put, the City of Nunapitchuk does not have a permitted landfill. Instead, solid waste is dumped in or near two adjacent tundra ponds, one for summer use and one for winter. Both sites are located across the river from the village, making them only accessible by boat or snow machine. The two sites are cut off each spring and eventually fail due to the river freeze breaking up. This unfortunate situation allows high amounts of standing water to infiltrate both sites, preventing them from becoming Department of Environmental Conservation acceptable landfills. The Seldovia wastewater treatment system does not meet current secondary wastewater treatment standards. The existing Seldovia sewer slough system is comprised of about 56 connections. Unfortunately, several faulty service connections to the system contribute to high Inflow and Infiltration. It is possible due to this high Inflow and Infiltration that no settling is occurring, and raw waste is being discharged into Cook Inlet. Shaktoolik uses two different access points in the Tagoomenik river to supply drinking water for the community. A winter source located near the city center is used for 8-9 months per year. A summer source which is located approximately 6,500 feet south of the city and is used for 3-4 months. A permanent installed four-inch diameter, insulated, heat taped line runs from the water treatment plant to the river bank near the winter source. A four-inch diameter, non-insulate, non-heat taped, HDPE pipe lying on the ground surface transports water from the summer source. The line is blown out at the end of the summer to prevent freeze-up and to ensure that the line is accessible the following summer. Water quality is often impacted at the winter source by salt water intrusion and high conductivity associated with high tides and storm events. Teller is a honey bucket community where most haul water using 5-gallon jugs from the existing water point in "Townsite". The community is split into two distinct areas; "Townsite" the original settlement, and "Newsite", the location identified 2 miles up-hill where housing was placed in the 70s after a severe flood. This location was chosen as the primary area for the community to expand. The problem is, Newsite has a soil profile that is very ice rich, which presents a challenge for piped water and sewer systems. Currently, only the clinic, school, and school housing have piped water and sewers. This leaves the rest of the community lacking proper sanitation infrastructure. Tuluksak is a village which has not been served with piped water and sewer. Residents use honey buckets, which are generally disposed of in neighborhood sewage collection bins. Sanitation operators then collect the waste and transport it to the waste disposal facility. When it comes to fresh water, only the clinic receives hauled water. Residents meanwhile, obtain water from a watering point and natural sources. At this time the water treatment plant cannot meet capacity requirements, which jeopardizes community health. Tununak is another village without piped water or a proper sewer management system. In fact, a water haul system serves only part of the community. Residents who are not served collect water at a single watering point operated by the local school, and from natural sources. Currently, the water treatment plant is not capable of meeting the requirements of the Surface Water Treatment rule. When it comes to sewage treatment, a flush-haul system serves only part of the community. An-on-site septic system serves only the washeteria, water plant, and sewage haul service. The other residents use honey buckets, which are generally self-hauled from the home and disposed of on the beach.
